title: You have health insurance. Why are you still fighting for care?
description: Team, A woman with breast cancer is under anesthesia. Her mastectomy has already begun. In another operating room, her reconstructive surgeon, Dr. Elisabeth Potter, is finishing a case when a nurse comes in with an unusual message: UnitedHealthcare is on the phone, and they need to speak to her right now . The call is about the woman currently undergoing surgery. The insurance company wants Potter to explain the patient’s diagnosis and justify why she needs to remain in the hospital overnight. The patient has breast cancer. She is already unconscious. Her surgery was authorized. Her physicians have determined the care she needs. And yet, in the middle of the operation, her surgeon is being asked to step away and defend it. Potter told me that in that moment she felt like she was having to “protect my patient from her insurance company.” The overnight stay was ultimately denied anyway, and the patient received a bill for $100,000 . After Potter spoke publicly about what happened and the story exploded online, she says the bill was erased. But that immediately raises a much more disturbing question: what happens to the patient whose doctor doesn’t have a viral video? Your nervous system needs inputs, too Taking an active role in your health also means paying attention to the stress you carry every day—and making room for recovery before you’re completely depleted. Between work, training, travel and caring for the people around you, “just relax” can feel like one more thing on an already unreasonable to-do list. That’s one of the reasons I’ve been using Nuropod .

title: A study of 854 women found one hormone linked to lower levels of Alzheimer’s-related tau
description: Team, For decades, we have spoken about menopause as though it happens below the neck: hot flashes, poor sleep and weaker bones. But estrogen loss reaches the brain—and ignoring that may be one of the greatest blind spots in women’s health. A new peer-reviewed study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia adds to the evidence that estrogen biology may be connected to one of the central processes underlying Alzheimer’s disease: the accumulation of tau. Researchers studied 854 female participants aged 50 and older from the European Prevention of Alzheimer’s Dementia Longitudinal Cohort. Their average age was approximately 65, and the group included cognitively healthy participants as well as people with mild cognitive impairment. Using a highly sensitive method called liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, the researchers measured two estrogens circulating in the blood: estradiol and estrone. They then compared those concentrations with three Alzheimer’s-related biomarkers measured in cerebrospinal fluid: Amyloid-beta 42, Phosphorylated tau 181 and Total tau. The clearest finding was this: higher circulating estradiol was associated with lower phosphorylated tau at baseline. The relationship was stronger in women who carried APOE4, the most important common genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease. This matters because abnormal phosphorylation changes how tau behaves inside the brain. Tau can detach from the internal structure of neurons and eventually accumulate into the tangles associated with Alzheimer’s disease and neurodegeneration.

title: I’ll Say it... GLP1’s are a Longevity Drug and they Work Better in Women than Men
description: Team, I was on FaceTime with my sister-in-law yesterday. She’s 47, she’s been trying for months to get back to the strongest version of herself, and she’s doing everything right, or everything she’s been told is right, and it isn’t quite working. So I mentioned GLP-1s. Gently. Just as one thing worth understanding. And her face changed. “Aren’t those the ones that make your hair fall out and eat your muscle?” She’d read the posts. The muscle loss, the thinning hair, the gaunt “Ozempic face.” She was scared of them, and she couldn’t actually tell me what they did or how they worked. She just knew she was supposed to be afraid. And I sat there thinking, this is one of the most-studied drugs in modern medicine, and one of the smartest women I know is terrified of it based on captions. That conversation is why I’m writing to you today. Because my sister-in-law is not unusual. She’s the rule. Most people I talk to are frightened of these drugs and fascinated by them at the same time, and almost nobody has been given the honest version. So let me give it to you. Because two days ago, something landed that changes the conversation entirely. A team at UC Berkeley took a group of old female mice, the mouse equivalent of a woman in her late 60s, and gave half of them a GLP-1 drug. The same class of drug as Ozempic and Wegovy. Not from youth. From old age. And the mice that got the drug lived meaningfully longer than the ones that didn’t. Their median lifespan went from 742 days to 834 days. That’s about 12% more life, and it was published in Nature two days ago (Feng et al., 2026). From Feng et al., Nature (2026), used under CC BY 4.0.
